implementation_notes: Node expresses the pattern as a threshold plus a return value: a Writable's highWaterMark is the buffer bound, write(chunk) returns false once the internal buffer reaches it, and 'drain' (or the writableNeedDrain flag) says when to resume - back-pressure without a queue class, as long as the producer actually stops. The documentation is explicit that highWaterMark is a threshold rather than a hard limit: chunks written while the stream is not draining keep buffering until Node aborts on maximum memory, so the hard bound is your loop, not the option. For a drop, reject or coalesce policy, keep a bounded array or use objectMode with your own counters and shed before calling write().
pitfalls: Ignoring write()'s false quietly removes the bound: Node keeps buffering past the threshold and aborts only on maximum memory, which is the outage the pattern exists to avoid.
Consuming a stream through 'data' listeners ignores back-pressure entirely; use pipeline()/async iteration (or explicit pause/resume) for the bound to hold.
highWaterMark counts bytes, objects or UTF-16 units depending on mode: for variable-size payloads size it deliberately or the 'bound' bounds the wrong thing.

variants.name: WHATWG WritableStream with a queuing strategy
variants.implementation_notes: In browser, worker, Deno and edge runtimes the standard primitive is a WritableStream built with a queuing strategy (CountQueuingStrategy or ByteLengthQueuingStrategy): the strategy's highWaterMark is the capacity, and once the internal queue reaches it the writer's ready promise stalls, so the producer is gated instead of buffering forever. Note the omission that bites: with no strategy the default behaves like a count of one, and the standard streams deliberately never drop - the drop, coalesce or reject decision stays application code, taken by checking the writer's desiredSize or by shedding before calling write(). Use abort(reason) for the explicit 'discard everything now' path.
pitfalls: Forgetting the strategy leaves the default high water mark of one, so the pipeline stalls constantly (or, if you set it absurdly high, buffers without a real bound).
write() returns a promise that can reject on abort/errored state: unhandled rejections turn a controlled shed decision into an unhandled rejection crash.
The streams API never drops for you - a 'bounded' stream with a producer that never checks desiredSize is simply an unbounded queue that applies back-pressure to nobody.
